name: MailerLite
tagline: Send newsletters, build forms, and run a small welcome sequence

pricing.notes: Typical starting monthly price at a small subscriber count.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 250 subscribers, 2,500 monthly emails, 2 seats, 1 website, 1 landing page, 3 forms, 3 active automations, 5 automation steps.
tiers.notes: 24/7 email and chat support for first 14 days.

tiers.name: Comfort
tiers.limits: Starting paid plan; 3 seats, email sends 10x subscriber tier, 50 automations, 100 steps, 10 sites/landing pages/forms, 5 products/bookings.
tiers.notes: Annual price uses official 10% yearly discount.

tiers.name: Power
tiers.limits: Unlimited monthly emails, unlimited user seats, unlimited sites/landing pages/forms/automations, 100 automation steps, 24/7 live chat.
tiers.notes: Annual price uses official 10% yearly discount; fair-use limits apply.

pricing.freeTierCaps: $0; 250 subscribers, 2,500 monthly emails, 2 seats, 1 website, 1 landing page, 3 forms, 3 active automations, 5 automation steps.
pricing.hiddenCosts: If you outgrow subscriber limit, billing can move to the next tier; Free locks sending above 250 subscribers; dedicated IP add-on on higher tiers.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For MailerLite, send newsletters, build forms, and run a small welcome sequence. The hard boundary is deliverability, editor polish, landing pages, automations, and integrations, plus deliverability, growth network, and integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Collect subscribers through forms, compose and send compliant newsletters and a small welcome sequence, publish a web archive, and report basic delivery and click events.
whatYouLose: deliverability, editor polish, landing pages, automations, and integrations
ongoingBurden: DNS authentication, reputation, bounces, complaints, unsubscribe compliance, templates, queues, analytics, backups, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for MailerLite because newsletter operators pay for inbox placement, growth mechanics, and operational confidence on publication day. The recurring cost buys DNS authentication, reputation, bounces, complaints, unsubscribe compliance, templates, queues, analytics, backups, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Listmonk
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source newsletter and mailing-list manager.

alternatives.name: Brevo Free
alternatives.desc: Campaigns, forms and automation with a 300-email daily throttle.

facts.dataFormat: Contacts, campaigns, consent records, and message events live in Brevo's cloud; contacts can be exported as CSV.
facts.gapVsPaid: Brevo Free covers campaigns, forms, and automation, but its 300-email daily throttle and weaker website/landing-page experience are worse than MailerLite.
facts.setupBlocker: Authenticating a custom sending domain requires adding DNS records.

alternatives.name: EmailOctopus Free
alternatives.desc: Newsletters, one form and a small welcome automation for 2,500 contacts.

facts.dataFormat: Lists, campaigns, automations, and reporting data live in EmailOctopus' cloud; contacts and reports can be exported as CSV.
facts.gapVsPaid: EmailOctopus Free works for newsletters and a welcome flow, but its limited forms, automations, and reporting are less complete than MailerLite's small-site toolkit.
facts.setupBlocker: You must verify a sender address or domain; DNS authentication is the first technical step.

alternatives.name: Kit Free
alternatives.desc: Forms, landing pages and one sequence for up to 10,000 subscribers; one recommendation slot is not yours.

facts.dataFormat: Subscribers, tags, forms, broadcasts, sequences, purchases, and analytics live in Kit's cloud; subscriber and chart data export as CSV.
facts.gapVsPaid: Kit Free provides forms, pages, and one sequence, but its one-automation limit and Kit-managed recommendation slot are less flexible than MailerLite.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no software install, but custom-domain sending requires DNS authentication and the free plan keeps one Kit-managed recommendation slot.

alternatives.name: MailPoet Starter
alternatives.desc: WordPress newsletters, forms and a basic welcome automation for 500 subscribers; WordPress is mandatory.

alternatives.name: Sender Free
alternatives.desc: A genuinely useful hosted list with forms, landing pages and workflows; branding remains.

facts.dataFormat: Subscribers, campaigns, automations, and engagement events live in Sender's cloud; subscriber data can be exported.
facts.gapVsPaid: Sender Free has a generous hosted allowance, but vendor branding and a weaker website-building surface make it less complete than MailerLite.
facts.setupBlocker: A custom sending domain must be verified with DNS records for reliable delivery.

rejectedAlternatives.name: listmonk
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A superb broadcast tool, but no built-in welcome sequence means it misses the stated job.

rejectedAlternatives.name: MailerLite Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free plan now stops at 250 subscribers; that is a demo with better posture.

rejectedAlternatives.name: SendPortal
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Commonly suggested, but its repository has been motionless since April 2024.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Growing Business plan and a single-publication newsletter DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for MailerLite in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Amazon SES; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: collect subscribers through forms, compose and send compliant newsletters and a small welcome sequence, publish a web archive, and report basic delivery and click events.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement subscriber import, double opt-in, unsubscribe, suppression, tags, and consent timestamps.
Create a Markdown campaign editor with HTML and plain-text previews.
Queue sends through SES with retries, rate limits, idempotency, and resumable batches.
Process delivery, bounce, complaint, open, and click webhooks without logging message content.
Publish a simple issue archive and subscriber preference page.
Add test sends, seed-list checks, DNS setup guidance, exports, and backups.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a newsletter recommendation marketplace.
Deliberately leave out ad sales and payment infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out complex lifecycle automation and enterprise deliverability support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
